clue.text: Alien beginning to eat toxic nuts

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so only the first letter is taken
nuts means crazy, so the letters go wild and rearrange themselves

explanation.surface: A strange creature starts eating poisonous nuts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nuts' looks like the food the alien eats, but it is the signal to rearrange TOXIC, which then follows E.
explanation.definitionFit: Exotic means foreign or from another country, which is the older sense of alien, not a creature from space.

clue.text: The other king from the south is Persian ruler

indicators.note: in a down entry, reading from the bottom means reading upwards, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: 'the other' is a coy British euphemism for sexual intercourse
Latin for king, as in royal signatures

explanation.surface: Someone notes that a different monarch, from southern lands, is a ruler of Persia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The other' reads like 'another', but it is the British euphemism for sex. SEX then REX, read upwards, gives XERXES.
explanation.definitionFit: Xerxes was the ancient king of the Achaemenid empire who invaded Greece in 480 BC.

clue.text: In game, small victory ends in frank exchanges

indicators.note: the ends of words are their final letters, so the last letter of each is kept

blocks.note: tiddly is British informal for very small

explanation.surface: During a match, a narrow win comes from some blunt words between the players.
explanation.walkthrough: Tiddly is British slang for tiny (it also means slightly drunk). TIDDLY + WIN + KS.
explanation.definitionFit: Tiddlywinks is a parlour game where players flick small plastic discs into a cup.

clue.text: Caught Old Nick, reportedly, displaying bladed weapons

indicators.note: what is reported is heard rather than read, so a word is swapped for one sounding the same

blocks.note: c is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
to nick is British slang for to steal; the metal sounds identical

explanation.surface: Someone claims to have caught the Devil himself brandishing knives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old Nick' looks like one name for the Devil, but the two words work separately; nick is British slang for steal, and the indicator applies only to it.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a literary term for swords, knives and bayonets, as opposed to firearms.

clue.text: I do parts playing in the style of others

definitions.note: describes what the person does rather than naming the person

indicators.note: playing about with something moves it around, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An actor explains that they play roles by imitating other performers.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads as the speaker's own description of the job; the first three words are the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A parodist writes or performs comic imitations, copying a particular writer's or performer's manner.

clue.text: Friend left without recycling bin, creating flipping diversion

indicators.note: recycled material is broken down and remade, so the letters come out in a new order
'without' in its old sense of outside, so one piece sits around another

explanation.surface: A mate went off without putting the recycling bin out, starting a crazy distraction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' is used in its old sense of outside, not lacking, so the friend-and-left pair wraps around the reworked bin.
explanation.definitionFit: The arcade game uses flippers to keep a steel ball in play, so it is an amusement worked by flipping.

clue.text: Quash underground resistance on return

indicators.note: returning means going back the way you came, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: the Tube is London's underground railway
R is the symbol for electrical resistance

explanation.surface: Authorities crush the wartime underground resistance movement when it comes back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Underground resistance' looks like one phrase about partisans, but it is two pieces: the London Tube and the physics symbol R, read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To rebut an argument is to refute or knock it down, close to quashing it.

clue.text: Pop art movement snubbed

indicators.note: snubbed suggests cut short, like a snub nose, so the tail is removed

explanation.surface: Pop Art, as a movement, was ignored by the critics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pop art' reads as one phrase, but Pop is the definition and the art movement is Dada, cut short.
explanation.definitionFit: Pop is an informal American word for father, just like the shorter family name.

clue.text: Appropriate fur coats nudist regularly ignored

indicators.note: a coat goes around what it covers, so one piece wraps another
skipping at regular intervals leaves every second letter

blocks.note: sable is the fur of a small Asian marten

explanation.surface: Fitting that fur coats are not worn by naturists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coats' looks like a plural noun, but it is a verb: the fur is wrapped around the letters left from nudist.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean right or fitting for a particular purpose or occasion; they are straight synonyms.

clue.text: Violet-grey network of lines next to ebbing African river

indicators.note: an ebbing tide flows back out, so the letters go backwards

blocks.note: a grid is a pattern of crossing lines

explanation.surface: A greyish-purple map grid lies beside a river going down in Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: An obscure colour word built from simple parts: GRID + NILE reversed.
explanation.definitionFit: The name, from French gris de lin (flax grey), is a rare word for a pale purplish-grey shade.

clue.text: Needle chap meeting family

blocks.note: bod is British informal for a person, short for body

explanation.surface: An irritating man goes to meet his relatives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Needle' looks like a verb (to annoy) describing the chap, but it is the noun definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A bodkin is a blunt thick needle with a large eye, used for threading tape or elastic.

clue.text: Boy will like Greece

blocks.note: he'll, a boy's 'he will', apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A lad is sure to enjoy a trip to Greece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Like' reads as a verb (to enjoy), but it is the preposition meaning 'as'.
explanation.definitionFit: Hellas is the Greek people's own ancient and modern name for their country.

clue.text: Main wrappers removed from rare item: bread in Saudi Arabia

indicators.note: unwrapping takes off the outer layer, so only the inner letters remain

blocks.note: bread is slang for money, and the rial is the Saudi currency

explanation.surface: The packaging is stripped off a rare loaf, the staple bread of Saudi Arabia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bread' looks like food, but it is old slang for money.
explanation.definitionFit: An arterial road is a main road, carrying traffic like the body's chief blood vessels.

clue.text: Uncompromising and concerning, like Lewis on eponymous TV series

blocks.clueFragment: like Lewis on eponymous TV series
blocks.note: Lewis, the former sidekick, got his own show after Inspector Morse ended, so he was without his old boss

explanation.surface: A TV review calls a detective show's lead tough and worrying.
explanation.walkthrough: Inspector Morse and its spin-off Lewis are British TV detective dramas; in Lewis, Morse is dead, so the sergeant is Morse-less.
explanation.definitionFit: Remorseless means relentless and pitiless, never letting up or giving ground.

clue.text: I'm travelling quickly in a small buggy to get microscopic creatures

blocks.clueFragment: I'm travelling quickly in a small buggy
blocks.note: surface reading: someone racing along in a little cart

blocks.clueFragment: I'm travelling quickly in a small buggy
blocks.note: setter's reading: a beast on wheels, the name of tiny pond organisms with a whirling crown of cilia

explanation.surface: A person whizzes along in a little go-kart.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the first part as a creature on wheels: an animal riding a buggy. The second half is a straight definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Rotifers are tiny aquatic organisms whose beating cilia look like turning wheels, giving them this common name.

clue.text: Healthy and mature farming system

blocks.note: not ill, read as one run of letters

explanation.surface: A farming method is praised as wholesome and well established.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Healthy and mature' looks like a description of the system, but it is the wordplay: NOT ILL + AGE.
explanation.definitionFit: It is an agricultural method of sowing crops without ploughing the soil first.

clue.text: Initiate fight very loudly, stopped by knockout

indicators.note: something stopped is plugged up, so another piece sits inside it

explanation.surface: A noisy boxing bout is started and then ended by a knockout.
explanation.walkthrough: SPAR + FF, with KO plugged into the second part: SPAR + KO + FF.
explanation.definitionFit: To spark off a chain of events is to trigger or set it going, a phrasal-verb synonym.

clue.text: Possibly rent rocks for crustacean

indicators.note: rocking things shakes them about, so the letters are shaken into a new order

explanation.surface: A sea creature may tear apart the rocks it lives among.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' looks like a hedging adverb, but both of the first two words are the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a clawless marine decapod with a spiky shell, also known as the rock lobster or crawfish.

clue.text: Device to contact doctor, say: buzzer on a clothes line

indicators.note: to clothe something is to cover it, so one piece goes around another

blocks.note: as in fifty pence a day, 'a' can mean per

explanation.surface: A pager is described as a buzzer pegged up on a washing line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clothes line' reads as a washing line, but clothes is a verb. In a down entry, 'on' puts the buzzer piece above the next.
explanation.definitionFit: A bleeper is a British name for a pager, the small radio device used to summon hospital staff.

clue.text: Minister to eat around six

indicators.note: going around something encloses it, so one piece surrounds another

blocks.note: to dine is to eat a meal

explanation.surface: A government minister has dinner at about six o'clock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minister' suggests politics, but here it is a clergyman, and 'six' is a Roman numeral rather than a time.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun, a divine is a cleric or theologian, a minister of religion.

clue.text: Address a gentleman restricting competition

indicators.note: to restrict is to hold in, so the letters are kept inside the words before

explanation.surface: A gentleman is spoken to about being banned from a contest.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run from the middle of 'Address' through 'a' into 'gentleman'.
explanation.definitionFit: Dressage is an equestrian event in which horse and rider perform precise set movements for judges.

clue.text: American priest secreted small insect

explanation.surface: A US clergyman produced a tiny bug from his body.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Secreted' suggests oozing a substance, but it means hid.
explanation.definitionFit: Aphids are tiny sap-sucking bugs, such as greenfly, that infest garden plants.

clue.text: False statement by great German chemist

explanation.surface: A notable German scientist has been misquoted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Great' looks like praise of the chemist, but it belongs to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Justus von Liebig was a 19th-century German scientist who founded organic and agricultural chemistry.

clue.text: Accompany group of women visiting barbarian

indicators.note: a visitor goes inside someone's home, so one piece enters another

blocks.note: the Women's Institute, a British countryside women's organisation
the Goths were Germanic tribes the Romans called barbarians

explanation.surface: A party of ladies takes a companion along when calling on a savage.
explanation.walkthrough: The Women's Institute is a British women's club famed for jam and charity calendars, and the usual crossword group of women.
explanation.definitionFit: To go with someone is to travel alongside them, an everyday phrasal synonym.

clue.text: Anger in 75% of country (or perhaps 43%?)

indicators.note: three quarters of a four-letter word means one letter is dropped

explanation.surface: Fury is felt by most of a nation, or maybe fewer than half.
explanation.walkthrough: Three letters of EIRE is 75%; the bracket jokes that three letters of IRELAND would be about 43%.
explanation.definitionFit: Ire is a literary word for rage or wrath, used mostly in writing.

clue.text: Spike welcomes surprisingly nice pacifist

indicators.note: welcoming a guest means taking them in, so one piece goes inside another
a surprise turns expectations around, so the letters come out in an unexpected order

blocks.note: a spike in a graph is a sharp high point

explanation.surface: Spike, a man's name, is pleasantly surprised to greet a peace campaigner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spike' looks like a person's name, but it means peak. Rearranged NICE goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Peacenik is informal, slightly mocking slang for an anti-war activist or someone opposed to violence.

clue.text: Criminal from American wing

blocks.note: US English for the wing or mudguard of a car

explanation.surface: A crook belongs to a US political faction or military unit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wing' suggests a faction or bird part, but it is the British word for a car body panel, which Americans call a fender.
explanation.definitionFit: An offender is someone who has broken the law, a general synonym for a lawbreaker.

clue.text: English largely behind festival

indicators.note: largely means for the most part, so the word loses its final letter

blocks.note: astern means at the back of a ship

explanation.surface: The English are mostly running late for a celebration.
explanation.walkthrough: ASTERN, a nautical word for behind, loses its last letter after E.
explanation.definitionFit: Easter is the Christian spring holiday celebrating the resurrection of Jesus.
